name: Coherence Must Improve 100x
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Clock Is Always Ticking: Why Qubits Need to Stay Quantum Longer
lesson.summary: A qubit's coherence time, how long it can hold onto its fragile quantum state before noise destroys it, needs to improve by roughly another order of magnitude or two beyond typical current values, in rough ballpark terms, for fault-tolerant machines to run the huge numbers of error-correction cycles that useful algorithms require.
lesson.body:
The earlier chapter on the decoherence problem explained that a qubit's quantum state, its superposition, its entanglement with other qubits, is fragile, and that interactions with the surrounding environment, stray electromagnetic fields, tiny vibrations, temperature fluctuations, gradually destroy that quantum information in a process called decoherence. A qubit's coherence time is, roughly speaking, how long it can be trusted to hold useful quantum information before decoherence corrupts it beyond recovery.

Coherence times vary enormously depending on the qubit technology, which makes any single number for the field misleading if stated without qualification. Superconducting qubits, the kind used by companies like IBM and Google, typically have coherence times reported on the order of tens of microseconds up to a bit over a millisecond in leading devices, with the best research-grade devices pushing somewhat beyond that. Trapped-ion qubits typically have much longer coherence times, in some cases reported at seconds or longer, but their gate operations also tend to run much more slowly than superconducting gates. That last point matters more than it might seem, because what actually determines how much computing a qubit can do is not its raw coherence time in isolation, but the ratio of coherence time to gate operation time, in effect, how many individual operations can be performed before the qubit's state decoheres.

That ratio is what fault-tolerant computing actually needs enough of, and it is worth explaining why the requirement is so demanding. Running a large fault-tolerant algorithm means performing not just the useful computation itself but an enormous number of additional error-correction cycles, repeatedly measuring and correcting errors across every logical qubit, potentially many times per logical operation, over the entire runtime of the algorithm. For a problem large enough to matter economically, that could mean billions of individual operations carried out over the full course of the computation. Every one of those operations has to complete within, in effect, the coherence budget available. If a qubit decoheres faster than the error-correction process can detect and fix problems, the computation fails, no matter how many physical qubits are available or how sophisticated the error-correcting code is.

The roughly one hundred times figure in this chapter's title should be read the same way as the error rate figure two chapters back: a rough, widely cited ballpark estimate from the field, not a precise engineering specification. Various estimates suggest that coherence times, or more precisely the ratio of coherence time to gate time relevant to running deep fault-tolerant circuits reliably, need to improve on the order of another one to two orders of magnitude beyond typical current values, commonly summarized as needing roughly a hundredfold improvement. The exact multiplier depends heavily on which platform, which specific device, and which underlying metric, raw coherence time versus effective number of operations survivable before failure, is being used, so this figure is best treated as a directional signpost rather than a fixed target.

It is worth closing this three-chapter cluster by tying the numbers together explicitly, since none of them stands alone. Error rates need to drop by roughly a hundredfold, physical qubit counts need to rise by roughly a thousandfold, and coherence needs to improve by roughly another hundredfold, and these three rough, widely cited estimates are not independent of one another. Better coherence tends to directly enable lower error rates, since a qubit that holds its state longer makes fewer mistakes per operation, and lower error rates directly reduce how many physical qubits are needed to protect each logical qubit, which in turn softens the qubit count problem. That interdependence is genuinely good news for the field's long-term prospects, since progress on one front tends to ease the others. But it also means that no single announcement, a new qubit count record, an improved coherence time in one device, should be read on its own as evidence that fault-tolerant, practically useful quantum computing has arrived. You now have a concrete, intentionally approximate technical yardstick, built from the field's own widely cited estimates rather than any single company's marketing, to hold every future quantum computing claim against.
